title: Global Pop
objective: After this level you can explain how pop music from Korea, Nigeria and Latin America went global.
summary: Pop crossed borders without English: BTS topped the Billboard 200 in 2018, Afrobeats (not Fela's Afrobeat) reached the Hot 100, and Despacito led the Hot 100 for 16 weeks.

cards.headline: In 2018, America's No. 1 album was sung mostly in Korean.
cards.body: BTS's Love Yourself: Tear topped the Billboard 200 album chart, the first time a K-pop act had done it. It's one of three stories in this level, from South Korea, Nigeria and Latin America, about pop crossing the world without switching to English.

cards.headline: K-pop: English came last
cards.body: BTS was assembled by producer Bang Si-Hyuk's Big Hit Entertainment, starting in 2010. They sang about self-love, individuality and empowerment, mostly in Korean, and topped the album chart that way. Their first English-language song, "Dynamite," only arrived in 2020, when it debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. The fame came first; the English came later.

cards.headline: Afrobeats: mind the "s"
cards.body: Afrobeats grew up in Nigeria and Ghana in the early 2000s, mixing highlife, dancehall and soca into upbeat dance pop about love, success and partying. Mind the "s": Afrobeat, without it, is Fela Kuti's 1960s and 70s blend of Yoruba music with jazz and funk, known for its political bite. In 2016 Drake's "One Dance," featuring Wizkid, topped the Hot 100 for 10 weeks, and in 2021 Nigeria's Burna Boy won the Grammy for Best Global Music Album.

mascot.line: One little letter, two different musics. Fela would want you to get it right.

cards.headline: Latin pop: the "Despacito" summer
cards.body: In 2017, Luis Fonsi and Daddy Yankee's Spanish-language "Despacito" (with a remix featuring Justin Bieber) led the Billboard Hot 100 for 16 weeks. That tied the record at the time, and no mostly non-English song had ever held the top spot longer. America's biggest singles chart no longer needed English to crown a winner.
